title: Beyond Tracing: Anticipatory Technical Exploitation and Smart Friction
gist: Drawing on a 2023 Ukraine investigation into a foreign GNSS chip inside a Russian copy of the Shahed-136 drone, CSIS proposes shifting export-control enforcement from reconstructing past procurement pathways to forecasting the next one via repeatable substitution assessments, and redefining success as shaping how adversaries adapt rather than counting denied shipments.

insights.claim: A 2023 Ukraine investigation found a foreign-developed GNSS chip inside the Russian-produced satellite navigation unit of one of the first Russian copies of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136 one-way attack drone.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that Western commercial components remain embedded in Russian mass-produced munitions despite export controls, sustaining pressure on component makers' compliance costs.
insights.quote: Inside its Russian-produced satellite navigation unit was a foreign-developed Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) chip.
insights.locator: Informed by more than a decade of documenting

insights.claim: Knowing how many navigation modules had reached a diversion network let investigators estimate when Russian stocks would be exhausted and a new procurement solution would become necessary, converting inventory math into a forecasting tool.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Component-flow accounting yields timing signals on when adversary procurement will pivot, which is actionable for compliance teams at candidate substitute suppliers.
insights.quote: Knowing how many navigation modules had reached the diversion network made it possible to estimate when existing stocks would likely be exhausted and when a new procurement solution would become necessary.
insights.locator: Working with the manufacturer made it possible

insights.claim: The core limitation of technical exploitation is temporal rather than analytical, because by the time a new procurement pathway appears in a recovered weapon the adversary has already adapted.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explains why sanctions regimes chronically lag; the fix is timing, not more investigative capacity or new authorities.
insights.quote: The limitation of technical exploitation is not analytical, but temporal.
insights.locator: For more than two decades, U.S. technical-exploitation programs

insights.claim: Recovered materiel reveals engineering dependencies, component criticality, production choices, manufacturing constraints, commercial availability, and substitution opportunities, not merely the past procurement path.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Battlefield forensics is an underexploited intelligence asset on adversary industrial constraints, usable to target future controls precisely.
insights.quote: It reveals engineering dependencies, component criticality, production choices, manufacturing constraints, commercial availability, and substitution opportunities.

insights.claim: Tracing and attribution should be reframed as the start of the analytical cycle rather than its conclusion.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The author's central reframing, repeated three times in the piece; signals the doctrinal direction enforcement agencies are being pushed toward.
insights.quote: Tracing and attribution should no longer mark the end of technical exploitation. They should mark the beginning of anticipation.
insights.locator: That experience exposed a broader limitation

insights.claim: After the Ostec Group was sanctioned, suppliers redirected equipment to a replacement Russian recipient while a Kazakhstan-based company made hundreds of shipments into the same network, documenting how fast designations are routed around.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A named case study of sanctions circumvention through third-country intermediaries; Central Asian transshipment remains the live enforcement gap.
insights.quote: After the Ostec Group was sanctioned, for example, suppliers redirected equipment to a replacement Russian recipient while a Kazakhstan-based company made hundreds of shipments into the same network.
insights.locator: Procurement networks respond by finding new suppliers

insights.claim: Every successful disruption changes the procurement environment, so procurement networks predictably respond with new suppliers, replacement intermediaries, different jurisdictions, commercial substitutes, and system redesigns.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Treat every sanctions action as generating a forecastable next-move set rather than a terminal outcome when modeling enforcement effectiveness.
insights.quote: Every successful disruption—whether a sanctions designation, a criminal prosecution, an export-control action, or a corporate compliance decision—changes the procurement environment.
insights.locator: Modern sanctions, export controls, and enforcement measures

insights.claim: Despite the predictability of adversary adaptation, policymaking remains largely reactive, with governments responding only after new procurement pathways have already emerged.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Identifies a persistent structural inefficiency in Western export-control regimes, which caps their realistic effectiveness against adaptive states.
insights.quote: Yet despite this predictable pattern, policymaking remains largely reactive.
insights.locator: They also adapt by substituting commercially available technologies

insights.claim: The proposed innovation is not new technique but a repeatable follow-on deliverable, a substitution assessment produced once a critical component or procurement pathway has been identified.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A low-cost, no-new-authorities reform that could plausibly be adopted quickly, changing the tempo of future designations and compliance warnings.
insights.quote: What is new is assembling those practices into a repeatable follow-on product: a substitution assessment.
insights.locator: The proposal is not that every underlying technique is new

insights.claim: A substitution assessment identifies technically compatible alternative components, likely procurement pathways, engineering implications, and observable indicators that would reveal emerging acquisition efforts before substitutes reach the battlefield.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Component makers whose parts are technically compatible substitutes for already-controlled items should expect early compliance outreach and heightened diversion scrutiny.
insights.quote: It identifies technically compatible alternatives, likely procurement pathways, engineering implications, and observable indicators that could reveal emerging acquisition efforts before substitute components appear on the battlefield.
insights.locator: Prepared once a critical component or procurement pathway

insights.claim: Closing the anticipation gap requires no new authorities, institutions, or investigative capabilities, only extracting greater policy value from information governments already hold.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Low implementation barrier raises the probability of adoption; the binding constraint is tasking and analyst attention, not budget.
insights.quote: Closing this gap does not necessarily require new authorities, institutions, or investigative capabilities.

themes.theme: Smart friction as the policy objective

insights.claim: The goal of export controls should be reframed from stopping technology flows to introducing frictions that make acquisition slower, more expensive, less reliable, more visible, and ultimately less effective.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Redefines the success metric for sanctions policy, which changes how effectiveness is reported and therefore how future control regimes are justified.
insights.quote: the objective is to introduce targeted frictions that make acquiring, integrating, and sustaining those technologies slower, more expensive, less reliable, more visible, and ultimately less effective
insights.locator: The objective is not to stop the flow of technology entirely

insights.claim: The Government Accountability Office has found that U.S. agencies lack clearly defined objectives linked to measurable outcomes for assessing the broader effectiveness of sanctions and export controls.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: An official finding that the effectiveness of the entire sanctions apparatus is unmeasured, which weakens confidence in claims that controls are working.
insights.quote: the Government Accountability Office has found that U.S. agencies lack clearly defined objectives linked to measurable outcomes for assessing their broader effectiveness
insights.locator: Sanctions and export controls are commonly assessed

insights.claim: The useful policy question is not whether adversary adaptation occurs but whether governments can influence how it occurs, deliberately channeling adversaries toward worse procurement choices.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shifts the debate away from the binary success-or-failure framing that has dominated sanctions criticism.
insights.quote: The objective is not to prevent adaptation—but to shape it.
insights.locator: For adaptive adversaries, a single denied acquisition

insights.claim: Forcing adversaries onto gray market suppliers raises their exposure to counterfeit products and newly established intermediaries become more visible to financial institutions and customs authorities, so friction degrades adversary weapons quality even when procurement continues.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A mechanism by which enforcement still pays off despite continued flows: degraded reliability and higher detectability of adversary supply chains.
insights.quote: Procurement may shift toward gray market suppliers with greater exposure to counterfeit products.
insights.locator: In practice, this means deliberately channeling adversaries

insights.claim: Governments should engage manufacturers of likely substitute components before those products become diversion targets, converting industry outreach from reactive to anticipatory.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Firms making technically compatible alternatives to already-diverted parts should expect government contact ahead of any incident, a compliance-cost signal for component suppliers.
insights.quote: Once technical exploitation identifies potential substitute technologies, governments should engage the manufacturers of those products before they become diversion targets.

insights.claim: Disruption strategies should be evaluated by whether they raise the adversary's engineering and procurement burden, since policies that force redesigns, extend qualification timelines, or reduce production reliability create real friction even without denying access.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Introduces engineering friction as an explicit policy target, which favors controls on hard-to-substitute components over broad category bans.
insights.quote: Policies that force redesigns, extend qualification timelines, increase counterfeit exposure, or reduce production reliability introduce meaningful friction even when technology continues to flow.

insights.claim: Success indicators should include engineering redesigns, supplier substitution, longer procurement timelines, greater gray market reliance, and increased counterfeit exposure, rather than denied shipments, seizures, and designations alone.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A concrete alternative metric set; if adopted, official sanctions-effectiveness reporting changes shape and past regimes look better than headline seizure counts suggested.

insights.claim: The framing that sanctions and export controls are an endless game of cat and mouse is rejected, on the argument that the next procurement pathway can be anticipated before it emerges.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A pushback against the growing view that export controls are futile, relevant to forecasting whether Western control regimes are tightened or abandoned.
insights.quote: Sanctions and export controls are often dismissed as an endless game of cat and mouse. They need not be.
